findings.issue: Every path-variant probe starts from a protected prefix (/api/orders/, /API/ORDERS, //api/orders, /api/admin/orders/..;/, /api/orders/%2e%2e/products). That direction can only land on the authenticated catch-all, so it proves very little. The bypass that matters runs the other way: a variant that matches a PUBLIC edge rule while the downstream normalises it into a protected handler. The gateway picks the route from the raw path, and permitAll rules such as GET /api/products/** and GET /api/sellers/* sit in front of services that also serve /api/admin/** and /api/seller/**. So GET /api/products/%2e%2e/admin/theme, /api/products/..;/seller/offers, /api/sellers/..;/admin/payouts or /api/auth/login/..%2f..%2fme would pass the edge and reach product-service, seller-service or auth-service. Today only the default StrictServerWebExchangeFirewall (400) and each service's own auth stop this, and nothing guards that firewall default. Neither the contract nor the summary in evidence.md ('No path variant passed through') proves it.
findings.fix: Add anonymous probes that start from a permit prefix and assert exactly 400 (not merely 'not passed'): GET /api/products/%2e%2e/admin/theme, GET /api/products/..;/seller/offers, GET /api/products/%2E%2E/%2E%2E/api/orders/1, GET /api/sellers/..;/admin/payouts, GET /api/sellers/me%2f, POST /api/auth/login/..;/me, GET /api/products/1%2f..%2f..%2fadmin/theme, GET /api/categories//..//admin/theme. Also add a positive check that GET /api/sellers/me/ (trailing slash) and GET /api/sellers/me;x=1 give 401 or 400, never a pass-through.

findings.issue: Q1 risk, recording it: /api/seller/** (product offers/products, inventory stock/warehouses, order shipments, and seller-service ledger, payouts, analytics, ads, feedback) needs only authentication at the edge, so a CUSTOMER token reaches every seller API. I spot-checked the downstream checks and they exist: inventory WarehouseController @PreAuthorize hasAnyRole(SELLER,ADMIN), order SellerShipmentController @PreAuthorize plus an approvedSellerId lookup, product SellerController and seller-service SellerService. The edge therefore adds no defence in depth for money-adjacent seller endpoints (ledger, payouts), unlike /api/admin/**. It is not an exposure today. The test pins this behaviour, so a later fix will require updating it on purpose, which is correct.
findings.fix: Record a backlog or tech-debt item (owner sign-off needed, production change) to add .pathMatchers("/api/seller/**").hasAnyAuthority("ROLE_SELLER","ROLE_ADMIN") before anyExchange. When that lands, flip sellerPathsAreAuthenticatedOnlyAtTheEdge to expect 403 FORBIDDEN for CUSTOMER and add the rule to EXPECTED_ROLE_RULES.

findings.issue: decide() probes each rule using only anonymous, ROLE_CUSTOMER and a fixed PRIVILEGED list, against a synthetic GET /x exchange. A future rule that admits an authority outside that list (say hasRole('WAREHOUSE')), or that depends on the exchange (an IP or header-based manager), is classed as DENY. rolePrefixesAreKnown only compares ROLE entries, and the self-check only requires /actuator/** to be DENY, so such a rule would escape the AC-9 'new role rule fails' guarantee.
findings.fix: Assert that the set of DENY entries is exactly {ANY /actuator/**}. That way any other rule classed as DENY fails with 'unknown rule kind, extend EdgeRules'.

findings.issue: The edge cases for HTTP method override are not probed. The gateway has no HiddenHttpMethodFilter today, but nothing asserts that a POST permit (POST /api/products/1/views, /api/support/chat, /api/ads/impressions) carrying X-HTTP-Method-Override: DELETE or ?_method=PUT is still treated by the edge as a POST. HEAD and OPTIONS are also only probed on a protected path, not on a GET permit next to a protected sibling.
findings.fix: Add one probe: POST /api/products/1?_method=DELETE and POST /api/products/1 with X-HTTP-Method-Override: GET, anonymous, both expecting 401. Also add HEAD /api/sellers/me expecting 401.

findings.issue: The reviewed permit list is sound: I found nothing public that should not be. The /api/sellers/* overlap with /api/sellers/me matches seller-service's own PublicSecurityConfig, and every GET /api/products/** and /api/categories/** handler is a catalogue read. However, several entries are unauthenticated endpoints that cost money or can be abused (POST /api/support/chat, /api/auth/otp/request, /api/auth/password/forgot, the POST ad click and impression beacons that may feed seller ad billing, POST /api/products/*/views). Their reasons say nothing about the abuse control, and the test runs with gateway.rate-limit.enabled=false.
findings.fix: Add the compensating control to each reason (for example 'rate-limited per IP by the gateway limiter; signature/dedupe downstream'), or open a backlog item to assert that these paths are covered by the rate limiter. No production change in this item.

summary: This change is test-only: there is no src/main or build.gradle diff and no new dependency. Signing keys are generated at runtime by TestKeys and served by a local stub JWKS. The only committed literals are a fixed UUID subject, example.com emails and an amr value of 'password'. No secret or PII is committed or printed, since the classification table prints only methods, paths and decisions. The contract reads the real authorizeExchange chain, compares it against a reviewed permit table with reasons, and checks that permits are routed, /api/admin/** is restricted to the four back-office roles, /actuator is closed and unmapped paths (including /internal/x) deny by default. That is a real improvement. I checked every reviewed permit against the controllers it opens and found none that should be private; the test reveals no live exposure. /api/seller/** being authenticated-only at the edge (Q1) is acceptable for now because inventory, order, product and seller-service each enforce the SELLER role themselves. I am recording it as a defence-in-depth gap on ledger and payout APIs that deserves a follow-up edge rule. I am requesting changes for one major gap. The path-variant probes only traverse from protected prefixes, but the realistic bypass traverses from a public prefix (GET /api/products/**, /api/sellers/*, /api/auth/login) into /api/admin/** or /api/seller/** of the same downstream service. Today only the WebFlux firewall default and downstream auth block that path, and the contract does not guard it. Adding about eight anonymous permit-prefix traversal probes that expect 400 resolves it. The other findings are minor hardening of the contract.
